```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(width = 90)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

Latent class growth analysis (LCGA), also known as group-based trajectory
modelling, is a person-centred approach used to identify distinct subgroups
of individuals who exhibit different patterns of change over time. When the
same individuals are measured repeatedly, LCGA assumes that the population
consists of a finite number of latent classes, each characterized by a
specific developmental trajectory. These trajectories describe how the
outcome of interest changes over time within each subgroup. Individuals are
assigned to latent classes according to their posterior probabilities of
membership, which indicate the extent to which their observed measurement
patterns correspond to each estimated trajectory (Nagin, 2005).

Similar to latent profile analysis, LCGA focuses on identifying meaningful
subgroups within a population, but rather than distinguishing individuals
according to their patterns of responses at a particular point in time, it
differentiates them according to their longitudinal patterns of development
(Scrucca et al., 2024; Saqr et al., 2024). A defining feature of LCGA is the
assumption that individuals within the same class share an identical
underlying growth trajectory. Accordingly, within-class variation in
individual growth parameters is constrained to zero, and deviations from the
estimated trajectory are attributed to random measurement error. This
assumption distinguishes LCGA from growth mixture modelling, which allows
individuals within the same class to vary in their growth parameters and,
consequently, in their individual developmental trajectories.

LCGA is a special case of mixture regression (see the
[mixture regression](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/mixture-regression.html)
article). Time is the predictor, and the class is shared by all measurements
of a person rather than assigned to each measurement separately. In latents
it is therefore fitted with `mixture_regression()`, with time on the right of
the formula and `class_level = "group"`; adding random effects through
`random` turns the same call into a growth mixture model.

The assumption of identical trajectories within a class is both the strength
and the limitation of the model:

- **Strength.** The model is simple, fast to estimate and, as a mixture
  regression, accommodates every outcome family of `mixture_regression()`:
  continuous scores, binary outcomes, counts and ordered ratings.
- **Limitation.** Individuals of the same kind rarely follow one trajectory
  exactly. When they vary around it, the model can represent that variation
  only by adding classes, and it therefore tends to identify more classes
  than there are kinds of individuals (Bauer & Curran, 2003).
  The growth mixture model adds random effects for that variation; it is the
  subject of the [growth mixture article](https://pak.dynasite.org/latents/articles/growth-mixture.html).

Fitting both models and comparing them with `compare_models()`, as the
growth mixture article does, is therefore advisable.

| Role | Argument | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Outcome, measured repeatedly | left of `~` | `score` |
| Time (any shape) | right of `~` | `wave`, `wave + I(wave^2)` |
| Person | `id`, with `class_level = "group"` | `student` |
| Kind of outcome | `family` | `"gaussian"`, `"binomial"`, `"poisson"`, `"negative_binomial"`, `"ordinal"` |
| What predicts the class | `membership` | `"motivation"` |

## The data

`growth_scores` is simulated so the answer is known: 300 students tested on up
to seven waves, of three kinds (improving, stable, declining), each student
varying a little around their kind's trajectory, with motivation predicting
the kind. Missed tests (about 12%) need no imputation.

```{r data}
library(latents)
head(growth_scores)
```

## Fitting and choosing the number of classes

Persons are the classified units, so `id` names them and
`class_level = "group"` keeps all of a person's measurements in one class.

```{r enumerate}
enumerate_regressions(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 1:5,
                      id = "student", class_level = "group",
                      n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
```

The BIC keeps falling up to five classes (from 13,276 with one class to
11,425 with five), although only three kinds of student generated the data:
the students' own spread around their kind's trajectory is absorbed by
additional classes. With these data the growth
mixture model, which models that spread, picks three. Here, to keep the
three kinds, the three-class model is read:

```{r fit}
fit <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 3,
                          id = "student", class_level = "group",
                          membership = "motivation", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
fit
```

Every table is a data frame from `get_results()`:

```{r tables}
get_results(fit, "classes")
get_results(fit, "membership")
get_results(fit, "recovery", data = growth_scores, truth = "trajectory")
```

The three classes are an improving trajectory (class 3, 31.9% of the
students, gaining 3.37 points per wave from 47.56), a declining trajectory
(class 2, 33.6%, losing 2.35 points per wave from 57.87) and a stable
trajectory (class 1, 34.5%, gaining 1.05 points per wave from 61.00). Higher
motivation lowers the odds of the declining class relative to the stable one
(odds ratio 0.36) and raises the odds of the improving class (odds ratio
1.87). Of the students assigned to the improving and declining classes, 92.6% and
95.0% were generated with those trajectories, whereas a quarter of the
stable class (26 of 104 students) are improving students, whose spread around their
trajectory the model does not represent.

## Seeing the classes

Every view of a trajectory fit is one `plot()` call. Each class's trajectory
with its confidence band, the observed class means, and a sample of students'
observed trajectories as thin lines (a band for the spread of students
around their class needs random effects, so it appears only in the growth
mixture model):

```{r trajectories, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit)
```

The same with one panel per class:

```{r facet, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, facet = TRUE)
```

Individual students, chosen across each class's range of classification
certainty: their observations and their class trajectory.

```{r individuals, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(fit, what = "individuals")
```

The coefficients with their intervals and p-values:

```{r coefficients, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(fit, what = "coefficients")
```

How confidently each student is classified, one bar per student:

```{r classification, eval = has_ggplot, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(fit, what = "classification")
```

## Curved trajectories

Any formula works. A quadratic lets each class bend; compare it with the
straight model fitted the same way (without `membership`):

```{r quadratic}
straight <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave, growth_scores, n_classes = 3,
                               id = "student", class_level = "group",
                               n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
curved <- mixture_regression(score ~ wave + I(wave^2), growth_scores,
                             n_classes = 3, id = "student", class_level = "group",
                             n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
compare_models(straight = straight, curved = curved)
```

These trajectories were generated as straight lines, and the BIC of the
curved model is 15.6 points higher: the additional curvature is not
supported.

```{r quadratic-plot, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(curved)
```

## Outcomes that are not scores

For outcomes that are not continuous scores, latent class growth analysis is
the available model: random effects for a binary, count or ordered outcome
require numerical integration, which the growth mixture model in latents does
not perform. An alternative for trajectories of categorical states is to
identify the state of each person at each occasion and model the resulting
sequences of states (López-Pernas & Saqr, 2023, 2024).

**Pass or fail.** Whether each test reached 60 points, with a logistic
trajectory per class:

```{r binary}
passing <- transform(growth_scores, passed = as.integer(score >= 60))
pass_fit <- mixture_regression(passed ~ wave, passing, n_classes = 3,
                               family = "binomial", id = "student",
                               class_level = "group", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(pass_fit, "coefficients")
```

Each class's probability of passing over the waves, and the coefficients:

```{r binary-plot, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(pass_fit)
plot(pass_fit, what = "coefficients")
```

**Ordered bands.** The score in four ordered bands, with a cumulative-logit
(proportional odds) trajectory per class (McCullagh, 1980): each class has its
own thresholds between the bands and its own slope over the waves.

```{r ordinal}
banded <- transform(growth_scores,
                    band = cut(score, c(-Inf, 52, 58, 64, Inf),
                               labels = c("low", "middle", "high", "top"),
                               ordered_result = TRUE))
band_fit <- mixture_regression(band ~ wave, banded, n_classes = 3,
                               family = "ordinal", id = "student",
                               class_level = "group", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(band_fit, "coefficients")
```

The plot shows each class's expected band (1 = low to 4 = top), and the
students' own bands over the waves:

```{r ordinal-plot, eval = has_ggplot}
plot(band_fit)
plot(band_fit, what = "individuals")
```

Counts work the same way with `family = "poisson"`, or
`family = "negative_binomial"` when the counts are more spread out than a
Poisson allows.

## Distal outcomes

`three_step()` compares the classes on a variable measured once per person,
using the bias-corrected three-step method (Vermunt, 2010; Bakk & Vermunt,
2016), which accounts for persons being classified with error. The trajectory model must be fitted without `membership` for this
correction:

```{r distal}
three_step(straight, data = growth_scores, outcome = "motivation",
           contrast = "pairs")
```

All three pairs of classes differ in motivation (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted
p-values below .001).

## Choices and warnings

- **Latent class growth analysis and growth mixture models.** When persons
  of the same kind vary around their trajectory, as they almost always do for
  scores, the growth mixture model is fitted as well and the two are compared
  with `compare_models()`; the growth mixture model is preferred when it fits
  better. Use latent class growth
  analysis for non-Gaussian outcomes, for a first look, and when within-class
  variation is not plausible.
- **Number of classes.** Read the BIC with the over-extraction above in mind;
  the bootstrap likelihood-ratio test (`enumerate_regressions(bootstrap =)`)
  simulates from the same model without random effects. It can also favour
  extra classes that absorb omitted within-class variation. Compare the
  random-effects model as well; the bootstrap does not repair misspecification
  of its null model.
- **Starts.** Several starts are used (`n_starts`), and the best likelihood
  should be reached more than once (the fit reports how many times).
